articles.title: DAF: Deterministic affinity-guided latent flow for flexible many-to-many multiphase liver MRI synthesis.
articles.abstract: Dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) provides a crucial basis for diagnosing focal liver lesions (FLLs) by quantifying liver hemodynamics. However, its clinical application is constrained by the safety risks of gadolinium-based contrast agents (e.g., allergic reactions and gadolinium deposition) and prolonged scan times. While synthesizing liver DCE-MRI from non-contrast images is a promising strategy, current generation models are hindered by architectural rigidity, inefficient feature fusion, and limited support for variable acquisition availability. To address these limitations, we propose deterministic affinity-guided flow (DAF), a unified framework for flexible many-to-many synthesis of missing liver MRI acquisitions. DAF utilizes a synergistic dual-encoder to extract multi-scale anatomical features, which are adaptively aggregated via an adaptive affinity fusion module with a dynamic affinity routing hub. This representation is used to guide the flow-based path in the latent space of a pre-trained vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE), which is modeled by a deterministic latent representation flow (DLRF). DLRF models synthesis as a deterministic ordinary differential equation trajectory. Partial unbalanced optimal transport provides an asymmetric coupling in which the source marginal is softly relaxed and the target marginal remains constrained; with a predefined latent initialization, inference is repeatable under fixed settings. We evaluate DAF on LMRxDiag, a large private multicentre liver MRI collection comprising 7,195 patients, with BraTS2021 used as a secondary cross-domain evaluation. For NC-to-DP synthesis, DAF achieved 26.69 dB PSNR and 92.04% SSIM, compared with 26.46 dB and 91.54% for controllable flow matching. In the reader study, DAF-synthesized multiphase MRI yielded an HCC diagnostic accuracy of 85.6% and an AUC of 0.938, compared with 68.0% and 0.751 using non-contrast MRI alone. These results support DAF as a flexible approach to missing-acquisition synthesis, while NC-to-DCE synthesis represents a clinically relevant special case for virtual contrast enhancement.

articles.title: Can we trust a positive PSMA PET/CT before the Phoenix threshold? Positive predictive value after primary radiotherapy for prostate cancer. A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT is increasingly used after radiotherapy, even before the Phoenix threshold. We assessed the positive predictive value (PPV) of PET-positive findings in this setting. METHODS: Patients restaged with PSMA PET/CT after primary radiotherapy were classified as Phoenix-negative (PSA rise < 2.0 ng/mL above nadir) or Phoenix-positive. Local findings were verified by histopathology or MRI, metastases by histopathology or follow-up imaging. A sensitivity analysis was restricted to histopathology only. PPV was compared between Phoenix groups. RESULTS: Of 833 patients, 724 were PET-positive; 263 local recurrences and 219 metastatic findings had a reference standard. PPV was 83.7% for local recurrence and 95.0% for metastases. Local PPV was lower in Phoenix-negative than Phoenix-positive patients (77.7% vs. 88.1%, p = 0.029), but not with histopathological verification (84.1% vs. 86.9%); metastatic PPV did not differ between groups (96.3% vs. 94.2%). CONCLUSION: Restaging PSMA PET/CT reliably identifies recurrence after radiotherapy, even before the Phoenix threshold is met.
articles.journal: Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging
authors: van der Voort van Zyp JRN

articles.title: AI-based contrast dose reduction in brain MRI: systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis of AI-generated post-contrast images.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the performance of AI algorithms in reducing gadolinium (Gd) administration in brain MRI by generating synthetic post-contrast images from low-dose inputs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Comprehensive searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase were conducted through April 17, 2026. Study screening, eligibility assessment, quality evaluation, and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Pooled peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) values were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic. These analyses were additionally followed by evaluations of the reported qualitative assessments. RESULTS: Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria, most of which used convolutional neural network architectures. The pooled PSNR was 32.91 dB (95% CI: 31.37-34.46; I² = 99.08%) across seven studies, and the pooled SSIM was 91.81% (95% CI: 89.33-94.30; I² = 99.69%) across six studies. Subgroup analyses stratified by contrast-dose reduction level, deep learning model type, and input modality did not identify consistent contributors to heterogeneity. Given substantial between-study heterogeneity, pooled estimates were interpreted descriptively. Across the qualitative assessments, synthetic images were generally rated as diagnostically acceptable or comparable to full-dose images for most tasks, although subtle differences in lesion conspicuity and artifact patterns were reported. CONCLUSION: AI models demonstrate promising technical performance for generating synthetic post-contrast brain MRI with high voxel-wise similarity to full-dose images at substantial contrast-dose reductions. However, marked heterogeneity, limited external validation, and the lack of clinically oriented diagnostic outcomes limit the interpretability and generalizability of current evidence. KEY POINTS: Question There is a need to determine how effectively artificial intelligence can reduce gadolinium use in brain MRI by generating synthetic post-contrast images from low-dose inputs. Findings Across 12 studies involving 3846 patients, AI-generated post-contrast brain MRI achieved pooled peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) values of 32.91 dB and 91.81%, respectively, with substantial between-study heterogeneity. Clinical relevance AI-assisted synthetic post-contrast imaging may substantially reduce gadolinium exposure in neuroradiology while preserving diagnostic confidence. However, high heterogeneity highlights the need for cautious interpretation and further multicenter standardization before clinical adoption.

articles.title: Greater DTI-ALPS reduction in normal pressure hydrocephalus compared with Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the magnitude of diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) reduction across normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), Alzheimer's disease (AD), and Parkinson's disease (PD), and to refine its interpretation across the fluid-dynamic spectrum. MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched on 2 March 2026. Studies reporting baseline ALPS indices in AD, PD, or NPH with healthy controls were included. Standardized mean differences were calculated using Hedges' g with random-effects models. Cross-disease differences were evaluated using independent Z-tests. RESULTS: Forty-nine studies contributing 50 datasets and involving 5318 participants were included. ALPS indices were reduced in all three disorders compared with controls. The pooled standardized mean difference was -0.95 (95% CI -1.16 to -0.75; k = 16; I² = 59.5%) in AD and -0.70 (95% CI -0.86 to -0.54; k = 28; I² = 78.8%) in PD. In contrast, NPH demonstrated a markedly larger reduction of -2.20 (95% CI -2.84 to -1.56; k = 6; I² = 82.0%). The distribution of study-level ALPS values showed NPH clustered at markedly lower values with minimal overlap with AD or PD. Consistent with this, summary-level (unadjusted) Z-tests indicated a larger reduction in NPH than in AD (Z = 3.63, p < 0.001) and PD (Z = 4.44, p < 0.001), whereas AD and PD did not differ significantly (p = 0.061). CONCLUSION: DTI-ALPS reductions were observed across AD, PD, and NPH, with a substantially greater though heterogeneous reduction in NPH. This pattern may reflect CSF fluid-dynamic disturbance, structural distortion of the ALPS measurement environment, or both, although its physiological basis and diagnostic utility require prospective validation. KEY POINTS: Question Do diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) alterations demonstrate distinct magnitudes and patterns across normal pressure hydrocephalus and major neurodegenerative disorders? Findings ALPS indices were reduced across all three disorders, with a substantially larger reduction in normal pressure hydrocephalus (Hedges' g = -2.20) than in Alzheimer's disease (-0.95) or Parkinson's disease (-0.70). Clinical relevance Beyond the diagnosis of normal pressure hydrocephalus, which is radiologically apparent, the magnitude of DTI-ALPS reduction may hold value as a marker of fluid-dynamic or structural severity and treatment response, warranting prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Muscle fat fraction and T2 as MRI biomarkers of cubital tunnel syndrome: a prospective pilot study.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cubital tunnel syndrome (CuTS) is a common and debilitating compression neuropathy of the ulnar nerve. Using MRI, the early effects on skeletal muscle might be quantifiable, enabling early diagnosis and curative surgery. Muscle oedema is quantified through T2 mapping, and lipoatrophy is quantified through muscle fat fractions (FF). This prospective cohort study aims to investigate whether CuTS changes the muscle T2 of FF. MATERIALS AND METHODS: 29 healthy controls and 19 patients awaiting surgery were scanned at 3.0 T. In the forearm and the hand, FF images were acquired via three-point Dixon and T2 measurements were made using a multi-echo spin echo sequence. Measurements were extracted from ulnar-innervated muscles (flexor carpi ulnaris, 1st dorsal interosseous and adductor policis) and a control muscle, brachioradialis. Between-group comparisons are made using linear methods, and 95% confidence intervals (CI) are computed. RESULTS: Patients with CuTS had prolonged T2 and elevated FF in their ulnar-innervated muscles, compared to controls. In patients with CuTS, the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle had 3 ms longer T2 (CI 0.49, 5.64), and the 1st dorsal interossesi and adductor policis had prolonged T2 (mean 5.59 ms [CI 1.61, 9.58] and 5.35 ms [CI 1.18, 9.51], respectively). Patients' flexor carpi ulnaris also had 2% higher fat [CI 0.25, 3.60] than healthy controls. There were no detectable differences in T2 or FF in the brachioradialis between patients and controls. CONCLUSION: We show that adults with CuTS have prolonged T2 in ulnar-innervated muscles and an elevated FF in the flexor carpi ulnaris. KEY POINTS: Question There is no reliable or quantifiable diagnostic tool for diagnosing cubital tunnel syndrome. Findings The ulnar-innervated skeletal muscles in adults with cubital tunnel syndrome exhibit increased fat fractions and prolonged T2, which are subclinical. Clinical relevance Quantitative MRI, specifically muscle T2 and fat fractions, may be an early biomarker of cubital tunnel syndrome and useful for selecting patients for surgery.

articles.title: The toothless molar tooth malformation: exploratory fetal MRI-based phenotypical assessment of cases with suspected Joubert syndrome.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The molar tooth sign (MTS) is based on maloriented superior cerebellar peduncles (SCPs), a deepened interpeduncular fossa, and vermian hypoplasia, which may be less clearly delineable prenatally. Phenotypic assessment of patients with suspected Joubert syndrome (JS) was conducted, and additional morphological characteristics of JS on fetal MRI were defined. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, phenotypic assessment was performed for patients with a fetal MRI-based suspected diagnosis of JS. Analysis of the fetal brain included detection of MTS, brainstem anomalies, elevation of the fastigium in the midsagittal plane, thickened SCP with a course parallel to the anterior/middle cerebral fossa in the parasagittal plane, cerebellar dysplasia, cephaloceles, and extracerebral ciliopathic manifestations. RESULTS: Eleven patients were identified and analyzed-three cases with genetic confirmation of JS, three with incomplete genetic testing, five without confirmatory genetic testing. Classical MTS was present in 55% of cases. Pathological appearance of the SCPs was observed in 73%, and dysplastic cerebellum and brainstem hypo- or dysplasia in 100%. Elevation of the fastigium was observed in 91%, cephaloceles in 46%, and extracerebral anomalies, especially renal, in 64%. All cases showed a hypo- and dysplastic vermis. CONCLUSION: This study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and accompanying anomalies commonly observed in patients with a suspected diagnosis of JS. JS can be suspected on fetal MRI even in the absence of classical MTS based on characteristic anomalies of the SCPs, brainstem, and cerebellum in combination with extracerebral anomalies supporting this diagnosis. KEY POINTS: QuestionWhat are phenotypical presentations of patients with suspected Joubert syndrome (JS) in fetal MRI and can JS be suspected in absence of molar tooth sign? FindingsJS can be suspected in fetal MRI without MTS based on characteristic changes in superior cerebellar peduncles, brainstem, and cerebellum and co-occurring extracerebral anomalies. Clinical relevanceThis exploratory study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and associated anomalies commonly observed in cases with suspected JS. These findings may aid counseling physicians in selecting appropriate pregnancy management for patients with suspected JS.

articles.title: A negative contrast-enhanced imaging in atypical ductal hyperplasia: Is the risk of upgrade low enough to avoid surgery? a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The management of atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) remains a clinical challenge. The use of contrast-enhanced (CE) imaging has been proposed to reduce the upgrade rates of ADH and minimize unnecessary surgical procedures. PURPOSE: This systematic review aims to estimate the pooled upgrade rate of ADH diagnosed through percutaneous biopsy in cases with a negative CE examination, independent of biopsy technique, needle size, imaging guidance. METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science databases was performed in December 2024. Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, or PRISMA, guidelines were followed. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies checklist was used to assess the risk of bias. Upgrades were calculated using random-effects meta-analysis based on the log risk-ratios. RESULTS: Out of 124 screened articles, 7 studies were included, providing data on 312 ADH lesions, including 145 cases with a negative CE-MRI. The pooled upgrade rate was 1 % (95 % [CI]: 0 %-4 %) for ADH lesions with negative CE imaging after biopsy. The pooled risk ratio was 8.80, with a statistically significant difference (p < 0.001) between positive and negative CE imaging. The overall sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were 0.95 (0.85-1.00), 0.75 (0.58-0.89), 0.62 (0.41-0.82), and 0.98 (0.93-1.00), respectively. CONCLUSION: Although the study cohort was relatively small, we found a pooled upgrade rate lower than 2 %, suggesting that conservative management rather than surgery may be justified for ADH with a negative MRI-imaging, as established for BI-RADS category 3 lesions.

articles.title: Adult pancreatoblastoma: CT findings of an uncommon tumor.
articles.abstract: Pancreatoblastoma is a malignant tumor, which accounts for less than 1% of all pancreatic neoplasms. Further, it is rarely seen in adults and has a poor prognosis with metastasis or local invasion is present in nearly half of adult patients at diagnosis, most often involving the liver. CT is the first-line modality for detection and surgical planning, yet the findings overlap those of more common pancreatic tumors. Pancreatoblastoma typically presents as a large exophytic mass in the pancreatic head with well-defined margins and an enhancing capsule. However, the capsule is often incomplete, and advanced tumors may show infiltrative borders. The mass is heterogeneous and may be solid or mixed solid and cystic, with calcification, enhancing internal septations, necrosis, hemorrhage, or potentially even internal vascularity. Pancreatoblastoma is mostly hypoattenuating relative to normal pancreatic parenchyma and shows progressive enhancement. Large tumors may cause biliary or main pancreatic ductal dilatation, tumor thrombus, or invasion of adjacent organs. Using pathologically proven adult cases, this pictorial review illustrates the spectrum of CT appearances of pancreatoblastoma and highlights the imaging characteristics of this rarely encountered tumor.

articles.title: Vertebral fracture screening: beyond spine health assessment.
Explainable multi-group dynamic causal distribution learning framework to disentangle common and specific dynamic effective connectivity across MCI stages.
articles.abstract: Brain functional networks exhibit an intrinsic architecture that is preserved across brain disorder groups, upon which different groups display distinct patterns of abnormal interactions. Exploring the common and specific network patterns is crucial for revealing common pathological mechanisms, group-specific alterations, and disease progression. Dynamic effective connectivity (dEC) characterizes time-varying causal interactions among brain regions and provides an effective means of investigating common and specific network patterns. However, the disentangled learning of common and specific dEC across multiple groups remains underexplored, limiting a systematic understanding of dynamic causal mechanisms in brain networks across disorders and disease stages. We propose an explainable multi-group dynamic causal distribution learning framework that integrates spatial and temporal information to identify common and specific dEC distributions among different groups. Experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively and robustly identifies causality and disentangles common and specific causal structures. When applied to real-world data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, the proposed framework uncovers common and specific dEC across mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stages. Results show that, as MCI worsens, the dEC within the visual network and among functional hubs of the default mode network remain stable, whereas dEC associated with episodic memory, emotional processing, and interoception shift from compensatory to decompensatory patterns. The code is available at https://github.com/OrangeLY-byte/EMGDCD.

articles.title: Spatial Heterogeneity of Brain Myelin Aging and Vascular-Metabolic Risk-Associated Alterations: An MR Fingerprinting Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize spatial patterns of age-related variation in MR fingerprinting (MRF)-derived myelin water fraction (MWF) and its associations with vascular-metabolic risk. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, neurologically asymptomatic adults underwent MRF scanning at 3T MR. MWF maps were estimated using a three-compartment model. Non-negative matrix factorization identified cortical gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) clusters in healthy participants; eight subcortical regions were analyzed separately. Generalized additive models were used to generate healthy reference curves. Deviations, aging slopes, and exposure-by-age interactions were compared between healthy controls and participants with vascular-metabolic risk. RESULTS: Among 285 participants (57.2 ± 14.4 years; 168 females), 167 were healthy and 118 had vascular-metabolic risk. Two cortical GM and two WM clusters with distinct aging patterns were identified. GM cluster 2 (frontal-parietal-occipital cortices) showed higher MWF with age, and WM cluster 2 (projection and association fibers) showed marked negative age association after midlife. Compared with healthy participants, the vascular-metabolic risk group had a less positive age association in GM clusters (cluster 1: β = -2.77 × 10-5/year, q = 0.046; cluster 2: β = -4.14 × 10-5/year, q = 0.034) and lower deviation from the healthy reference in WM cluster 2 (β = -0.00351, q = 0.036). Continuous blood-pressure main effects on deviation were nonsignificant after FDR correction, but complementary tertile analyses showed more negative age-related slopes in the highest than the lowest tertiles in WM cluster 2 and the subcortical summary (all FDR-corrected q < 0.01). CONCLUSIONS: MRF-derived MWF imaging revealed regionally distinct myelin aging patterns and selective deviations linked to vascular-metabolic risk, particularly in projection and association WM fibers. Blood pressure may be relevant to regional myelin-related aging patterns, warranting validation in larger longitudinal cohorts.

articles.title: Motor pre-selection modulates action observation effects in sensorimotor cortices: a MEG study.
articles.abstract: According to the Motor Simulation theory, observing an action automatically activates matching motor representations. This can explain why, in automatic imitation tasks, responses are faster when the observed action matches the required one, compared to when it differs. However, the automatic imitation task setting represents a very peculiar situation where participants need to pre-select the motor representations corresponding to the actions that they might observe, a situation quite different from daily-life contexts such as sports (e.g., tennis or basketball) where actions pre-selected for output are typically different from those observed, and where imitation errors or tendencies are seldom observed. This leads to the following question: Does the motor cortex response to observed actions depend on whether they match the motor representations pre-selected for output? In the present magnetoencephalography experiment, we studied, within the hand-related primary sensorimotor cortex, the oscillatory dynamics produced by the observation of hand actions in two conditions: either while participants pre-selected motor representations similar to those observed, or while they pre-selected markedly different motor representations, such as those involved in feet actions. Our data show that the motor cortex reacts differently to action observation in the two pre-selection conditions: alpha- and beta-band activity showed stronger desynchronization when the pre-selection involved motor representations matching those observed compared to non-matching ones. Specifically, observing hand actions while pre-selecting non-matching feet movements elicited a late rebound-like increase in alpha- and beta-band activity that was not observed when hand actions were pre-selected.

articles.title: Preoperative prediction of microsatellite instability in rectal cancer using multiparametric MRI-derived intratumoral heterogeneity and exploration of biological mechanisms: a multicenter study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a machine-learning model combining multiparametric MRI-derived intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) scores with clinical features for preoperative prediction of microsatellite instability (MSI) in rectal cancer and to explore MSI-associated molecular features. METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled 464 rectal cancer patients from three centers, including training (n = 198; MSI-H, 26), internal validation (n = 110; MSI-H, 12), and external validation (n = 156; MSI-H, 23) cohorts. Three-dimensional ITH scores were derived from T2WI and DWI. Logistic regression identified independent clinical predictors. Six machine-learning algorithms were used to construct clinical, ITH, and combined models. Performance was assessed using AUCs with 95% confidence intervals, calibration curves, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP. TCGA transcriptomics, PPI analysis, and immunohistochemistry in 10 local samples were used for molecular exploration. RESULTS: Age, tumor length, location, and N stage were independent predictors. The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.865 (95% CI, 0.828-0.899), 0.839 (95% CI, 0.775-0.895), and 0.785 (95% CI, 0.729-0.835) in training, internal, and external cohorts, respectively. In external validation, it was comparable to the clinical model (AUC = 0.790; BH-adjusted P = 0.076), and the ITH-only model performed poorly (AUC = 0.548). SHAP identified tumor location, T stage, and ITH features as major contributors. Transcriptomics identified 378 differentially expressed genes, and PPI analysis suggested AKT1 as a hub candidate. IHC showed higher AKT1 H-scores in MSS tumors (143.60 ± 26.14 vs. 76.74 ± 38.43; P = 0.008). CONCLUSION: The model showed favorable training/internal performance but moderate external performance without clear incremental value. Larger prospective multicenter cohorts are needed. Transcriptomic and pilot IHC analyses suggest possible AKT1 expression differences between MSI-H and MSS rectal cancers.

articles.title: Familial ACOX1-related neurodegeneration with progressive demyelination: Clinical and NODDI findings in two siblings.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in the ACOX1 gene result in neuronal loss due to peroxisomal disorder and elevated very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA). On the other hand, a recurrent monoallelic gain-of-function variant (p.N237S) in ACOX1 has been associated with neurodegeneration, skin rash, hearing loss, and peripheral neuropathy, a condition known as Mitchell syndrome. METHODS: Herein, we report on two siblings with ataxia, cognitive decline, progressive demyelination, and normal VLCFA who share a missense variant in the ACOX1 gene (p.R490G) in heterozygosis inherited from their clinically asymptomatic mother. RESULTS: Brain MRI showed progressive demyelination and callosal hypoplasia. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) analyses showed that the probands' intraneurite fraction is smaller than that of their parents. Also, the orientation dispersion index in the probands was smaller. CONCLUSION: These results show that diffusion MRI microstructure modeling may be a useful tool for diagnosis and follow-up of hypomyelinating conditions.

articles.title: Comparison of atlas-based and artificial intelligence-based methods for bone age assessment in a pediatric population: agreement and influencing factors.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools are increasingly used for bone age assessment, but their agreement with traditional atlas-based methods requires further evaluation. OBJECTIVE: To compare bone age estimates obtained using the Greulich and Pyle Atlas, the Pocket Atlas of Skeletal Age, and the Hand Bone Age AI web application developed at Stanford University. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed in 376 pediatric patients. Agreement between methods was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, Friedman tests, and subgroup analyses according to age, sex, and pubertal status. RESULTS: Median bone age estimates were identical across methods (144 months). Overall agreement was high (ICC=0.93, 95% CI 0.92-0.94). Significant differences were observed between the AI-based method and both atlas-based methods, whereas no significant difference was found between the two atlas-based approaches. Clinical agreement within ±12 months reached 96.5% for the atlas-based methods and 77.4-83.8% for comparisons involving AI. Sex significantly influenced agreement, while pubertal status showed less consistent effects. CONCLUSION: AI-based and atlas-based methods showed high overall agreement, although AI demonstrated greater variability at the individual patient level. Patient sex may influence agreement between assessment methods.

articles.title: Taenia-Tela choroidea complex in Joubert syndrome and Chiari 2 malformation.
Enhanced prognosis stratification following surgery for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to optimize clinical decisions by reflecting tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has an extremely dismal postoperative prognosis. Conventional TNM staging cannot adequately characterize tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment, leading to suboptimal risk stratification. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an integrated prognostic system for PDAC by combining deep learning (DL)-based radiomic features with guideline‑recommended clinicopathological variables. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included 592 patients with PDAC who underwent R0 surgical resection. A Swin Transformer-assisted DL classifier (Outcome Prediction for PDAC, OP-PDAC) was built using multi-planar contrast-enhanced CT scans (axial, coronal, and sagittal planes). Radiogenomic analysis was conducted in 41 patients to elucidate the biological underpinnings of the OP-PDAC. Furthermore, the Intelligent Prognosis Stratification System (IPSS-PDAC) was developed by incorporating clinicopathological variables into the OP-PDAC framework. RESULTS: In the derivation and test cohorts, the C‑index of OP-PDAC for predicting 1‑year disease‑free survival (DFS) ranged from 0.807 to 0.844, which was significantly higher than that of the clinicopathological model (CP-PDAC; C‑index, 0.631-0.656). The IPSS-PDAC further enhanced predictive performance, yielding a C‑index of 0.836-0.871, and enabled effective stratification for both DFS and overall survival (all log‑rank p < 0.01). Radiogenomic analysis revealed that high‑risk patients exhibited an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, elevated stromal scores, activated oncogenic pathways, and reduced CD8+ T‑cell infiltration. CONCLUSION: IPSS-PDAC is a non-invasive and robust prognostic stratification system that integrates imaging features and clinicopathological features. By sensitively reflecting tumor heterogeneity and TME, it provides references for clinical decision-making in the postoperative management of PDAC patients. KEY POINTS: Question This study constructs an integrated prognostic model combining imaging signatures and guideline-recommended clinicopathological variables to address unmet clinical challenges in postoperative risk stratification for PDAC patients. Findings A multi-planar Swin Transformer-based deep learning model (IPSS-PDAC) achieves a C-index of 0.836-0.871 for disease-free survival prediction. Critical relevance statement High-risk patients stratified by the OP-PDAC model display a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, activation of core oncogenic signaling pathways, and reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration.

articles.title: Association of popliteal artery wall index with cartilage morphology and loss in knee osteoarthritis: data from the FNIH Biomarkers Consortium.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate MRI-derived popliteal artery wall index in relation to knee cartilage volume and 24-month cartilage loss in the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH) Osteoarthritis Biomarkers Consortium cohort. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This observational cohort study included 594 participants with one indexed knee each. Mean wall index was calculated by averaging values derived using the Fully Automated and Robust Analysis Technique for Popliteal Artery Evaluation across all evaluable axial cross-sectional images reformatted from the sagittal three-dimensional dual-echo steady-state MRI volume. Fully adjusted models, including relevant clinical and imaging covariates, evaluated cross-sectional and change-on-change associations with regional cartilage volume. Mixed-effects and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. RESULTS: At baseline, each 10-percentage-point higher mean wall index was associated with lower lateral femoral cartilage volume (β = -67.4 mm3; 95% CI, -126.4 to -8.3; p = 0.025) and thickness (-0.091 mm; 95% CI, -0.162 to -0.021; p = 0.011). Each 1-SD increase in mean wall-index change was associated with greater medial tibial (β = 0.53 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.95; p = 0.012) and lateral femoral (β = 0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.69; p = 0.048) cartilage-volume loss. The medial tibial association was supported by mixed-effects, robust, rank-based, and baseline-adjusted sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSION: A greater 24-month increase in mean wall index was associated with greater concurrent medial tibial cartilage-volume loss. Mean wall index derived from standardized 3D DESS knee MRI may provide complementary information about concurrent cartilage loss, although further longitudinal studies are needed to establish its clinical significance.

articles.title: Five-compartment restriction spectrum imaging for noninvasive assessment of liver fibrosis in chronic liver disease.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Noninvasive staging of liver fibrosis is essential in chronic liver disease (CLD). Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is well validated but requires dedicated hardware, whereas the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) derived from conventional diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lacks specificity. Restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) decomposes the diffusion signal into multiple compartments and may capture fibrosis-related microstructural changes. PURPOSE: To investigate the feasibility of RSI for noninvasive liver fibrosis staging in CLD and to compare its diagnostic performance with that of MRE, using liver biopsy as the reference standard. METHODS: This retrospective study included 100 consecutive patients with CLD who underwent liver biopsy, 3.0-T multi-b-value DWI (nine b values, 0-1500 s/mm²), and MRE within 6 months. Multi-compartment RSI models (K = 2-5) were fitted to region-of-interest-averaged signals, and the optimal model was selected using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). An RSI liver fibrosis index (RSI-LF) was derived from compartment fractions using ordinal logistic regression and internally validated with 1000 bootstrap resamples. AUCs of RSI-LF were compared with those of MRE and ADC using the paired DeLong test. RESULTS: The five-compartment RSI model (RSI5) showed the lowest BIC. The second and fourth fractions, K5C2 and K5C4, correlated positively (ρ = 0.53) and negatively (ρ = -0.55) with fibrosis stage (both false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.001). RSI-LF yielded AUCs of 0.774 (95% CI: 0.651-0.898), 0.863 (0.793-0.933), and 0.911 (0.842-0.981) for ≥F2, ≥F3, and F4, respectively, with negligible bootstrap optimism. AUCs did not differ significantly from those of MRE at any threshold (all p > 0.05). RSI-LF also outperformed ADC at the ≥F3 and F4 thresholds (both p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Five-compartment RSI provides diffusion metrics associated with histologic fibrosis stage, and RSI-LF showed diagnostic performance numerically comparable to that of MRE. RSI is a promising microstructure-sensitive biomarker for liver fibrosis staging that warrants multicenter validation.

articles.title: Diagnostic performance of liver virtual non-contrast and virtual unenhanced reconstructions derived from photon-counting detector CT of the upper abdomen.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) enables native spectral imaging with the generation of virtual non-contrast (VNC) images from contrast-enhanced acquisitions. Two reconstruction algorithms are currently available, Virtual Unenhanced (VUE) and Liver Virtual Non-Contrast (LVNC), but their reliability compared with True Non-Contrast (TNC) imaging in abdominal applications remains incompletely established. This study evaluated the quantitative accuracy, image quality, and potential clinical impact of VNC reconstructions derived from PCD-CT. METHODS: In this retrospective single-center study, 150 patients, of whom 140 were included for the analyses, underwent multiphasic PCD-CT including TNC, arterial, and portal venous phases. VNC datasets were generated from arterial and venous acquisitions using the VUE and LVNC algorithms. Tissue attenuation, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were compared with TNC images. The agreement of VNC reconstructions with TNC-based classification criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis, and osteoporosis was also evaluated. RESULTS: Significant attenuation differences were observed between TNC and VNC reconstructions across most tissues. The smallest errors were found in soft tissues, particularly the liver and spleen, whereas the largest discrepancies occurred in vascular and osseous structures. SNR was higher on VNC than on TNC images in the liver, spleen and paravertebral muscle but lower in several other tissues, whereas CNR was higher with LVNCa and lower with VUEv than with TNC. VUE most closely reproduced TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs. Agreement with TNC-based criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis and osteoporosis required reconstruction-specific cut-offs, which should be considered exploratory. Omitting TNC could potentially reduce radiation exposure by 16.5% for upper abdomen and 21.2% for total abdominal examinations. CONCLUSIONS: VUE reconstructions showed good agreement with TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen in both contrast phases, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs and was closer to TNC than VUE only in subcutaneous fat and venous-phase muscle. Substantial bias in vascular and bone structures limits the interchangeability of both algorithms with TNC imaging. VNC may support a potential reduction in radiation dose when replacing a planned TNC acquisition; since lesion detection and characterization were not evaluated, the safe omission of TNC was not demonstrated.
